questions.q: Why isn't "build us a dashboard that shows at-risk deals" already a usable requirement?
options: It doesn't mention Salesforce by name
"At risk" is ambiguous, so two people building from it could build different things
Dashboards cannot technically be built in Salesforce
It is too short to be a valid requirement regardless of content
questions.explain: A usable requirement has to be specific enough that two different builders would build the same thing. "At risk" could mean several different, non-interchangeable definitions until it's pinned down.

questions.q: A support manager asks for a bulk-close button for cases. What should an architect do with that request?
options: Build exactly the button requested without further questions
Reject the request because stakeholders shouldn't propose solutions
Hear the proposed solution, but keep asking questions to find the actual underlying need it's meant to serve
Escalate it directly to a developer without any clarification
questions.explain: A proposed solution might be right, or might be treating a symptom instead of the real problem. The architect's job is to understand the actual underlying need before committing to the stakeholder's proposed fix.

questions.q: What is the "why" ladder technique used for?
options: Prioritizing a backlog of already-clear requirements
Repeatedly asking why a stated request matters, to surface the real business driver underneath it
Assigning story points to a user story
Deciding which Salesforce license type a new user needs
questions.explain: The why-ladder pushes past the first stated request, one "why" at a time, until the underlying business outcome the stakeholder actually cares about becomes visible.

questions.q: In the lesson's deal-dashboard example, what did three rounds of "why" actually reveal the real need was?
options: A faster-loading dashboard UI
An earlier, more reliable signal that a deal is heading toward trouble
More sales reps hired
A new CRM entirely, replacing Salesforce
questions.explain: The repeated why-questions revealed that a dashboard was only one possible way to deliver what the business actually needed: an earlier warning signal before a deal was already lost, which could be served by several different solutions, not just a dashboard.

questions.q: Which of these captures all three things a well-written, handoff-ready requirement should state, per this lesson?
options: The requester's job title, their manager's name, and the project's budget
Who needs it and why, what "done" looks like in observable terms, and any already-known constraint
The exact Apex class name and SOQL query that will implement it
A list of every Salesforce object currently in the org
questions.explain: A requirement that survives a handoff states the underlying business driver (who/why), an observable definition of done, and any known constraint (deadline, data volume, existing system) — enough for someone else to build the right thing without needing the original conversation.
